Docs/Internal Architecture

Internal Architecture

◆

NOTE: This is a first draft, information here is volatile and may not be perfectly accurate.

This page goes over semi-important internal details which may matter when building a page.

The Two Worlds

Elegance builds every page twice:

  • Server code - which is imported at request-time (or build-time) by Node. Contains init, data fetching, server actions, page rendering.
  • Client code - this is shipped to the browser as bundle.js. Contains view, onMount, onUnmount, onNavigate, event handlers, and atoms.

Both are derived from the same source file, split apart by a source transform.

The Pages Pipeline.

Let's start with a page: pages/page.tsx.

tsx
const UNUSED_VARIABLE = 1234;

const BUILD_TIME = Date.now();

export default function Page() {
    return <main>This page was built at: {BUILD_TIME.toString()}</main>
}

We'll also have our root layout of course: pages/layout.tsx

tsx
export default function Layout({ children }) {
    return <>{children}</>
}

When you run elegance, esbuild bundles this page, the result of which looks something like this:

js
// put the actual bundled result here (including layout ofc)

This code is then passed to our oxc-based transformer, which generates 2 versions of the same page; serverCode and preClientCode.

The server code is written and cached as route_(pathname).server.mjs, and is imported in the runtime. The pre-client code will go through more processing later, but is for now stored in route_(pathname).pre_client.mjs.

These files are all available in your config.outputDirectory/cache. It can be useful to check it if you're curious about how things work in Elegance, or if you're trying to fix bugs.

The pre-client code is finally built into a bundle.js by generateSynetheticBundle, which modifies the pre-client code by wrapping it in a synthetic page() constructor function, and generates the required static regions and handlers (more on these later)

The end bundle will look something like this:

js
/// put bundle here

If two routes import the same file, the file get's split into a chunk, which are visible in config.outputDirectory/dist/chunks/.

Once the page is sent, the browser imports client.js, and the given pages bundle.js (and it's chunks)

esbuild Specifics

  • Pages & Layouts are bundled per-route with bundle: true, format: "esm", packages: "external". Bare packages stay external by default. Read more about DCE & Bundling here
  • esbuild injects a // path/to/file comment before every inlined module — these source path markers are what keep server/client transforms consistent (see Source Path Markers).
  • A custom plugin (eleganceBundlePlugin) decides which third-party packages get inlined instead of staying external (see Third-Party Bundling).

The Oxc Transform

We run an OXC transform over the output that esbuild generates. The transform outputs two variants of the same source via three edit sets.

  • shared edits - which are applied to both server and client.
  • server-only edits - which are only in serverCode.
  • client-only edits - which are only in preClientCode.

Key Rewrites

Component ID Injection

To get a stable ID for each component (without the user having to specify one), we inject an __id param for every call to the component() function.

js
component({
    __id: "ABC-123",
    view() {
        return div("Hello World!");
    }
});

Global Atom Rewrites

Atoms in the server-code get a stable injected ID as their first param. On the client, they're translated to _getAtom(<id>) calls, which fetches the value of the atom from the IAV payload.

ts
// Original:
const counter = atom(0);

// Server:
const counter = atom("ABC-123", 0);

// Client
const counter = _getAtom("ABC-123");

Tag Calls

For convenience sake, in elegance we use function-style element call tags, like div(). However, to avoid collisions, these must be renamed to __tags.xyz() on both the server and the client.

This step also applies to JSX, where <div></div> becomes __tags.div().

In this same step, any serverAction call is replaced with _action(<id>); and init() callbacks are removed from pre-client code.

Dead Code Elimination (DCE)

The client bundle is aggressively pruned to only what's reachable from the page:

  • Seeds — the page's default export, component() declarations, _getAtom() declarations, onPageLoad closures, and element handlers.
  • Reachability walk - starting from the recorded seeds, every referenced binding is marked reachable. Unreachable declarations, functions, and imports are cut from the final code.
  • Because the walk runs on the final assembled bundle, code from inlined packages, layouts, and shared chunks is handled identically to page code, which let's people write things like component libraries.

Read more about DCE & Bundle generation here

Regions

Regions are the SSR → client hydration manifest.

  • When the server renderer hits a live component, it emits <template data-region="N"> at that position and pushes the component's descriptor into ctx.regions[N].
  • generateSyntheticBundle serializes those descriptors into the page's bundle.js as RLE-compressed entries: { __cid, props, children, count }.
  • On the client, hydrateWithRegions scans the DOM for template[data-region] markers, recreates each component instance from its entry, and reconciles it against the server-rendered DOM.
  • props and children are serialized as code (not toString), so the client re-runs view() with identical input to the server.
  • Consecutive identical entries are collapsed with count (run-length encoding).

Handlers

  • Element handlers (onClick etc.) are extracted from the pre-client source into { eid, handlers } records.
  • eids are assigned in render order on both server and client so they always match.
  • On hydration, the client binds the extracted handler functions to DOM elements via [e-id="..."] and a delegated event listener on document.

Hydration On The Client

  • component() registers component configs in a componentConfigs map, keyed by __id.
  • hydrateWithRegions turns each region entry into a synthetic live descriptor and calls bootstrapComponent.
  • Each instance holds its own props, children, atom objects, and dependency set.
  • execView runs the component's view with { self, atoms, children }; every atom read is tracked and marks the instance dirty on write.
  • Dirty instances re-run view() in a microtask and patch the DOM with a vdom morph (patch / morphKids).

Source Path Markers & IDs

  • esbuild's per-module // path comments become a sorted list of markers inside the transform.
  • Every __id/atom id is a hash of source path + call index.
  • Because server, client, layout, and chunk pipelines all read the same markers, the same component produces the same id in every artifact — this is what makes hydration and cross-page chunks work.

Atoms

  • On the server, atom() registers into the import context and its value lives in a render context.
  • On the client, _getAtom() restores values from the serialized initial-state payload (<script data-tag="iav">), then tracks reads/writes per instance.
  • Atom ids are generated by the oxc transform and must match between the server payload and the client registry.

Third-Party Bundling

  • By default all bare package imports are external.
  • A package can declare "elegance": { "bundle": [...] } in its package.json to opt its own paths into being inlined.
  • A project can do the same per-project in elegance.config.ts via bundling.include.
  • The esbuild plugin resolves each bare import, checks the owning package's declaration, and returns external: false on a match.
  • Banned paths (elegance.no-bundle in a package, bundling.noBundle in config) are passed to the DCE as globs; reaching them from client code is a build error.

Chunks & Shared State

  • Code splitting hoists shared modules into /chunks/* files.
  • Because of the ESM module cache, a shared chunk is evaluated once, so atoms defined in shared modules keep their state across pages and across client-side navigations.
